edges.effect_quant: Meal-based studies are inconsistent: some calcium supplements reduced dietary non-heme iron absorption by roughly 28% to 55%, whereas whole-diet crossover data found no significant reduction.
edges.population: healthy women consuming calcium with meals
edges.mechanism: Calcium can acutely interfere with intestinal uptake of both heme and non-heme iron, but that inhibitory signal competes with other features of the meal and may attenuate over repeated whole-diet exposure. This is why tightly controlled single-meal studies often look stronger than longer mixed-diet designs.
edges.summary: Calcium taken with meals probably has a small inhibitory effect on non-heme iron absorption in some settings, but the real-world magnitude is inconsistent. The evidence is strong enough to avoid a cleanly neutral label, yet too mixed to support a high-confidence harmful claim across whole diets.
edges.caveats: The effect depends on calcium dose, salt form, meal composition, and whether absorption is measured from a single challenge meal or a mixed diet over several days. This is best interpreted as a context-dependent absorption interaction, not a universal rule that all meal-time calcium meaningfully worsens iron balance.

evidence.citation: Cook JD et al 1991 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: Calcium supplementation: effect on iron absorption.

evidence.citation: Grinder-Pedersen L et al 2004 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: Calcium from milk or calcium-fortified foods does not inhibit nonheme-iron absorption from a whole diet consumed over a 4-d period.

evidence.citation: Gaitan D et al 2011 J Nutr
evidence.notes: Calcium does not inhibit the absorption of 5 milligrams of nonheme or heme iron at doses less than 800 milligrams in nonpregnant women.
